synthesis.headline: The south-central heat ridge holds but flattens as its western trough weakens; the day's storminess piles onto the ridge's north and east flanks, and the medium range keeps retreating the ridge toward the Southwest and northern Mexico
synthesis.narrative:
The amplified summer dipole Tlaloc has tracked for well over a week runs on, but with a notable softening in one half of it. The southern heat ridge is intact — this morning's 500 mb analysis puts a broad, relatively flat ridge over the south-central and southeastern US with heights near 594 dam along the Gulf Coast — while the western trough that was deep and near-cutoff yesterday has flattened into a long, low-amplitude, open trough from the Pacific Northwest through the Great Basin, not meeting blocking criteria. The center of gravity of the day's weather has correspondingly shifted east: the eastern-stream disturbance has matured into a well-developed extratropical cyclone with a comma-head and deep convection over the Ohio Valley and interior Mid-Atlantic. At the surface, a strong high dominates the central High Plains (the WPC analyst flags the plotted 1046 mb as almost certainly a misread — likely 1026-1036 — so treat the exact value with caution), a weak low sits over the central southern Plains, and Gulf dewpoints in the mid-70s pool the richest moisture across the lower Mississippi Valley and Gulf Coast. Canada carries real weight today: a broad ridge covers the western provinces while a deep 993 hPa low over Quebec/the Gulf of St. Lawrence drags a trailing cold front south with a tight gradient and northwesterly flow into Ontario and the northeastern US.

The centers of action still ring the ridge's northern and western rims, with the eastern cyclone now added on top. The most dangerous story remains the heat: WPC keeps a locked-in, multi-day hazardous heat wave over the southern tier, spreading into the Carolinas by Monday with heat indices near 115 and Major-to-Extreme HeatRisk — its convective suppression coming from midlevel subsidence and warming, a strong cap and dry air aloft, not from any surface high. Along the ridge's north flank a heavy-rain, severe, and flash-flood corridor runs from the Midwest through the central Appalachians and central High Plains, with a Moderate Risk for excessive rainfall over the Midwest/Ohio Valley Saturday-Sunday and West Virginia Sunday. SPC's Slight Risk covers the central High Plains (supercells and multicell lines off the Rockies, wind and hail) and the middle Ohio Valley (wet microbursts as a vort max reignites afternoon convection). Monsoonal moisture keeps a separate flash-flood threat going across the Interior West and Four Corners. Offshore, a compact, apparently independent convective cluster sits over the western Atlantic off the Carolinas, distinct from the continental system, though a single frame can't establish its organization.

The upper-level structure ties it together. The most prominent feature on the wind field is a 95-115 kt jet streak sweeping from the upper Midwest through the Great Lakes into the Northeast, curving anticyclonically toward New England — this is what is translating the eastern trough and its cyclone downstream and keeping the East progressive. The Air Mass RGB shows the ridge's signature: a broad red-orange plume of dry, subsident mid/upper-tropospheric air over the southern Plains, Gulf, and Southeast (warm-season ridge, not a stratospheric intrusion), with the sharp airmass boundary from the central Plains into the Great Lakes marking the implied jet corridor and baroclinic zone under the convective shield. A compact, intense reddish signature near the Colorado/New Mexico border reads as a possible localized dry intrusion wrapping into a shortwave — consistent with the small closed contour over Wyoming and the High Plains storm threat, though its scale warrants caution. On the regime question — whether the heat ridge is transitioning or merely being nudged — the two ensemble leads answer consistently and reinforce the last several days' message. The 6-10 day (Aug 20-24) puts its zero anomaly line through roughly 110-100°W, keeps the western CONUS near neutral, runs the positive-anomaly axis from the north-central Pacific into Alaska/BC, and flattens the East toward zonal. The 8-14 day (Aug 21-27) then retreats the ridge core even farther south and southwest, bulging the 588 dam contour across the Desert Southwest and northern Mexico with positive anomalies concentrated there and off Baja, while western Canada and the northern Rockies show no ridge and the East lies under a broad neutral-to-weakly-negative zone beneath a downstream trough. That is a genuine geographic contraction and southward retreat of the ridge toward the Southwest and northern Mexico, not a collapse and not a rebuild over the north — and both leads now agree on a deep cold low over the Canadian Arctic Archipelago, resolving the high-latitude disagreement flagged yesterday.
synthesis.climate_context: This is peak-summer North America running close to the seasonal script: the North American Monsoon is active across the Southwest and southern Rockies, and severe-weather season is being expressed as ridge-periphery, northern-stream convection along a wavy frontal zone rather than classic Plains supercells. The ENSO backdrop is a developing-to-established warm state — the ONI has climbed out of last year's weak La Niña (near -0.6) through neutral late winter into decisively warm territory, reaching +1.39 by May-July 2026, indicating a developing El Niño. That configuration typically favors the East Pacific while shear and dry air suppress the Atlantic, and today's tropics fit the split as the basin nears its early-September peak: the East Pacific is busy with Tropical Storm Lala east-southeast of Hawaii, Tropical Depression Hernan off Baja, and two disturbances each given 30% over seven days, while the Atlantic stays quiet, with a southeastern-Caribbean wave expected to stay disorganized and a central-Atlantic wave at just 10%, both fighting strong upper winds and dry air. Teleconnections are only a directional cross-check in summer and are mixed today — the NAO has turned distinctly negative (-0.90), which would favor eastern blocking and is broadly consistent with the amplified downstream trough, but the AO has swung positive (+0.37), stepping away from high-latitude blocking, and the PNA is weakly negative; the summer weakness of these indices warrants caution in leaning on any one of them.
synthesis.regional_notes: SPC reports no active mesoscale discussions, so the severe signal stays at outlook level: central High Plains supercells with wind and isolated large hail into mid-evening, wet microbursts over the middle-upper Ohio Valley, weak-shear pulse storms with occasional damaging gusts over the central Appalachians into the Carolinas and Georgia, and predominantly elevated overnight storms across the central Plains/mid-Mississippi Valley. The dominant regional hazard is hydrologic — the Moderate Risk excessive-rainfall corridor over the Midwest/Ohio Valley (with West Virginia added Sunday) plus a monsoon flash-flood threat over the Four Corners and Interior West favoring burn scars and steep terrain. In eastern Canada, the deep 993 hPa low over Quebec/the Gulf of St. Lawrence and its trailing front drive a tight gradient and gusty northwesterly flow across Ontario into the northeastern US.

sources.title: Surface Analysis
sources.summary:
Valid 1200Z Saturday 15 August 2026.

The most prominent surface feature is a 1046 mb high centered over the central High Plains, which is an unusually high reading for August at that latitude — the contour label appears to say 1046, but that would be extraordinary for a warm-season surface high; it more likely reads 1026 or 1036, and the precise value should be confirmed against surrounding isobars before asserting it. A second high of around 1025 mb sits over the upper Great Lakes region, and a 1022 mb high occupies the southeastern Gulf Coast states. A weak low near 1013 mb is positioned over the central southern Plains, with an associated stationary or slow-moving front trailing southwestward; a cold front extends from a low near the upper Midwest southward through the central Plains, meeting warm and moist surface air — dewpoints in the mid-70s F are plotted across the lower Mississippi Valley and Gulf Coast, placing the richest moisture axis there. The tightest isobar spacing, implying the strongest surface pressure gradient and wind forcing, appears along the Pacific Northwest coast near a 1034 mb high and a 1016 mb low pair, as well as along the cold frontal zone cutting through the Great Lakes toward the Mid-Atlantic, where a secondary low near 1016 mb is positioned off the Northeast coast; across the interior West and central Plains, the gradient is comparatively slack, limiting organized surface-based lift outside the frontal corridors.

sources.title: Canadian Surface Analysis
sources.summary: This CMC surface analysis for 0000Z 15 August 2026 shows a broad high pressure ridge dominating much of central and western Canada, with the 1019 hPa high centered over what appears to be the interior of British Columbia or southern Alberta, and a second high near 1025 hPa positioned over the central prairies region consistent with Saskatchewan or Manitoba, producing a relaxed gradient and generally settled conditions across the western provinces. Along the eastern seaboard and into Atlantic Canada, a trailing cold front extends southward from a low near 993 hPa positioned over what the isobar geometry places roughly over Quebec or the Gulf of St. Lawrence, with tightly packed isobars on the fronts western flank suggesting an area of enhanced gradient and likely northwesterly flow over Ontario and into the northeastern United States. Across the northern tier of the domain, several lows in the 996 to 1009 hPa range are distributed over the high Arctic and the approaches to the Canadian Archipelago, which is entirely consistent with typical summer Arctic cyclone activity and should not be read as unusual; their placement well poleward of the mainland provinces is clear from the chart geometry. In the lower 48, a sprawling area of relatively low pressure covers much of the central United States, and the frontal boundary connecting northward into Canada appears to separate warmer, moister air over the Great Plains from drier continental air to the northwest, implying a zone of potential lift along that boundary as it crosses into southern Manitoba or Saskatchewan, though the exact provincial border position is uncertain at this map scale. Tropical storm Lala is annotated at 17.4N 151.9W in the lower left corner of the chart, well out in the central Pacific and posing no direct Canadian relevance at this time.

sources.title: 500 mb Analysis
sources.summary: At 500 mb valid 1200 UTC 15 August 2026, the dominant feature across the CONUS is a broad, relatively flat ridge axis over the south-central and southeastern United States, with heights near 594 dam over the Gulf Coast region where a surface high (marked H) is positioned over the lower Mississippi Valley. The western half of the country shows a long, low-amplitude trough from the Pacific Northwest southward through the Great Basin, with heights around 583-589 dam along the West Coast; this trough is open, not closed, and the contour spacing and orientation suggest a neutral to slightly negative tilt across the interior West. The most prominent jet activity on the chart is the color-shaded wind corridor sweeping from the upper Midwest through the Great Lakes and into the Northeast, where speeds implied by the shading reach 95-115 knots, consistent with a well-defined jet streak oriented southwest-to-northeast and curving anticyclonically toward New England. The small isolated closed green contour over the northern Rockies or Wyoming area warrants notice — it appears to be a minor shortwave disturbance, but the single closed contour and limited shading make confident identification uncertain. Overall the pattern is progressive in the East with the jet streak translating the northeastern trough downstream, while the western trough is slow-moving and low-amplitude, not meeting the geometric criteria for blocking.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB (GOES-19)
sources.summary: Valid 15 August 2026 at 1331Z, this GOES-19 Air Mass RGB covers the CONUS and adjacent waters. A broad red-orange signature dominates the southern Plains, Gulf of Mexico, and Southeast, consistent with dry, subsident mid- and upper-tropospheric air under what is likely a warm-season ridge rather than a stratospheric intrusion. The sharpest airmass boundary runs roughly from the central Plains northeast into the Great Lakes region, where the transition from red-orange to green and then to white cloud mass marks the implied jet corridor and associated frontal zone. Along and north of that boundary, an organized comma-head structure with bright white cold tops is visible over the Ohio Valley and interior Mid-Atlantic, indicating a well-developed extratropical cyclone with active deep convection on its poleward and eastern flanks. A compact bright-white convective cluster sits over the western Atlantic off the Carolinas, appearing distinct from the continental system and suggestive of an independent area of deep convection, though its organizational context is not determinable from this single frame. Over the central Rockies near what appears to be the Colorado-New Mexico border, a small, intense reddish signature stands out against the surrounding greens, which on this product could indicate a localized dry intrusion wrapping into a shortwave trough, but the compact scale warrants caution before further characterization.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB Full Disk (GOES-19)
sources.summary: This GOES-19 Air Mass RGB from 1320Z 15 August 2026 shows a broad expanse of green (tropical moist airmass) dominating the tropics from roughly the Gulf of Mexico south through the Amazon basin, with scattered clusters of white deep convective tops embedded along and near the ITCZ over the eastern Pacific and across northern South America into the Atlantic. A compact, well-organized cyclonic system is visible over the western North Atlantic near the U.S. mid-Atlantic coast, its curved white cloud shield and darker blue cold upper airmass wrapping into the low center. Across Canada's Hudson Bay region and into the northwestern Atlantic, a sharp blue-to-green airmass boundary marks the polar front, with a strongly curved baroclinic cloud band consistent with an active extratropical cyclone tracking northeast off Atlantic Canada. In the Southern Hemisphere, active extratropical systems with bright white frontal cloud bands are apparent south of Argentina and across the South Atlantic, embedded within a deep blue southern polar airmass. The broad orange-red tones over the subtropical eastern Pacific and over the western interior of the continent are consistent with dry, subsident upper-tropospheric air under the summer subtropical ridge rather than stratospheric intrusion signatures, as they lack the compact elongated geometry characteristic of high-PV filaments.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day Temperature Outlook
sources.summary: The dominant signal is a broad above-normal temperature forecast covering essentially the entire contiguous United States, with the highest probabilities concentrated across the south-central states. A core centered roughly over Louisiana, Mississippi, and adjacent portions of Texas and Arkansas carries the 90-100% probability tier, indicating the model guidance is in strong agreement on well-above-normal temperatures there through August 20-24. Probabilities step down through the 70-80% and 60-70% tiers as you move outward toward the northern Plains, the interior West, and the Southeast Atlantic coast, which are still solidly above-normal but with somewhat less certainty. The lone exception on the mainland is a near-normal signal across the upper Great Lakes and portions of the Northeast, suggesting a modest intrusion of cooler air or simply weaker ridging influence at that range. In Alaska, western areas are forecast below normal while the interior and Panhandle lean above, implying a trough-ridge couplet over the North Pacific and Gulf of Alaska that, taken together with the persistent south-central U.S. heat signal, is consistent with a sustained amplified ridge over the southern tier rather than a regime transition within this forecast window.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary:
This is indeed a CPC 6-10 day 500 mb height and height-anomaly forecast, valid 20-24 August 2026, with green solid contours showing heights at 60 dam intervals and dashed contours showing departures from normal.

The dominant feature is a strongly negative anomaly center over the Canadian Arctic Archipelago and adjacent waters, where the closed low in the green height field sits near 534 dam and the anomaly dashed contours indicate a departure of roughly -90 dam — that magnitude is almost certainly a misread of units or scale; the contours labeled in what appear to be single-digit intervals suggest the anomaly values plotted are in meters, not dam, so the actual departure is likely on the order of -9 dam, which is a meaningful but not extreme negative anomaly. A positive anomaly region, with dashed contours suggesting roughly +9 dam, arches across the north-central Pacific and into far northwestern North America, implying a ridge axis running from the northeast Pacific toward the Alaskan panhandle and British Columbia. Over the contiguous western United States and into the central Plains, the anomaly field crosses near zero, with the zero line appearing to bisect roughly the 110-100°W longitude band, meaning any positive anomaly signal does not extend deeply into the interior West. The ridge axis tilts northeastward and the flow over the lower 48 broadly amplifies from west to east before flattening into a more zonal pattern across the central and eastern U.S., where heights of 582-594 dam dominate and anomalies trend slightly negative or near zero across the southeast.

sources.title: CPC 8-14 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary: This chart is a 500 mb height and height-anomaly forecast, but it plots absolute heights (green solid contours at 60 m intervals, labeled in meters — e.g., 5340, 5400, 5460 up through 5940 m, equivalent to roughly 534 to 594 dam) alongside anomalies (dashed contours, red positive, blue negative). The dominant feature is a deep, closed cold low centered over the Canadian Arctic Archipelago near 75-80N, with a core height around 534 dam — an unusually low value for August that implies a strongly negative anomaly there, consistent with the tightly packed blue dashed contours surrounding the center. Western Canada from British Columbia through Alberta and Saskatchewan shows strongly confluent height contours sweeping from the northwest with no evidence of a ridge axis over the northern Rockies or northern Plains; instead the implied flow is broadly cyclonic and the positive anomaly contours (red dashed) are conspicuously absent over that region, indicating a negative or near-normal anomaly across western Canada and the northern Rockies rather than the ridge that would drive heat into that area. The ridge axis and strongest positive anomalies are displaced well to the south and southwest, with the 588 dam contour bulging across the southwestern United States and northern Mexico, and the red dashed positive anomaly contours concentrated over the Desert Southwest and the eastern Pacific off Baja, confirming the ridge core has retreated far to the south rather than remaining anchored over the northern Rockies or northern Plains. The eastern United States lies in a broad neutral to weakly negative anomaly zone beneath the amplified downstream trough implied by the cyclonic curvature over the Great Lakes and Northeast.

sources.title: WPC Short Range Forecast Discussion
sources.summary: A locked-in pattern sustains multiple hazards through early next week. An upper high over the southern tier maintains dangerous heat spreading into the Carolinas by Monday, with heat indices reaching 115 degrees and Major to Extreme Heat Risk levels. Repeated severe thunderstorms, heavy rainfall, and flash flooding continue along a corridor from the Midwest through central Appalachians and central High Plains, driven by a mid/upper-level trough progressing eastward. Moderate Risk for excessive rainfall maintained for Midwest/Ohio Valley Saturday-Sunday; West Virginia under Moderate Risk Sunday. Monsoonal moisture in the Interior West and Four Corners may produce heavy rainfall and flash flooding in vulnerable terrain through the weekend.

sources.title: SPC Day 1 Convective Outlook
sources.summary:
Slight risk of severe thunderstorms across central High Plains and middle Ohio Valley through mid-evening Saturday.

Central High Plains: Storms developing over Rockies will move onto plains with moderate buoyancy and 30-35 kt effective shear supporting supercells and multicell lines. Primary threats are severe wind gusts and isolated large hail through early-mid evening.

Ohio Valley: Slow-moving MCS over central Illinois will weaken as low-level jet diminishes, but vorticity maximum drifting eastward should spark renewed development over middle-upper Ohio Valley as afternoon heating destabilizes the air. Threat is wet microbursts with damaging gusts.

Central Appalachians/Carolinas/Georgia: Abundant moisture and strong heating will create moderate buoyancy, but weak shear limits organization. Occasional damaging gusts possible.

Central Plains/Mid-Mississippi Valley: Elevated storms expected tonight with marginal shear; isolated strong-severe potential but predominantly elevated mode limits overall threat.

sources.title: SPC Mesoscale Discussions
sources.summary: No mesoscale discussions currently active. SPC is not tracking any organized convective threat at this time.

sources.title: NHC Tropical Weather Outlooks
sources.summary:
Atlantic: A tropical wave in the southeastern Caribbean produces gusty winds and showers with no development expected due to strong upper-level winds and dry air. A second tropical wave in the central Atlantic midway between Cabo Verde and the Lesser Antilles shows limited development potential before encountering strong upper winds; 10 percent 7-day formation chance.

East Pacific: Tropical Storm Lala east-southeast of Hawaii and Tropical Depression Hernan southwest of Baja California are under advisories. Two areas of low pressure may develop mid-week: one south of Mexico and another west-southwest of Baja, each with 30 percent 7-day formation chances and gradual westward movement expected.

sources.title: ENSO State (Oceanic Niño Index)
sources.summary: ONI values show La Niña conditions currently in place with anomalies around -0.6°C, gradually weakening through early 2026. By spring 2026, anomalies turn positive, transitioning toward neutral and then El Niño conditions by late spring/early summer. The MJJ 2026 value reaches +1.39°C anomaly, indicating developing El Niño. Overall trend is a clear shift from cool to warm phase over the next eight months.

sources.title: Teleconnection Indices (PNA, AO, NAO)
sources.summary: PNA is weakly negative and falling (7-day mean -0.70, down from -0.29), offering minimal directional signal in summer. AO has swung sharply positive (7-day mean +0.37, up from -0.05), shifting away from high-latitude blocking conditions. NAO has turned distinctly negative (7-day mean -0.90, down from +0.19), now favoring blocking patterns that could trap eastern systems. The NAO trend is the most notable change; summer teleconnection weakness warrants caution interpreting any single index.
